WHAT YOU’RE SEEING

A LITTLE EXPERIMENT

Count what stays the same.

Choose fission. Count protons and neutrons on each side of the reaction. A nucleus can split, but electric charge and nucleon number stay balanced.

Inside this model +

Fusion example: deuterium plus tritium produces helium-4, one neutron, and 17.6 MeV. This is a fusion research reaction; the Sun mainly uses the proton–proton chain.

Fission example: uranium-235 absorbs a neutron and splits into barium-141, krypton-92, and three neutrons. This is one possible product channel, not the only one. The Q value for this specific ground-state product channel is about 173.3 MeV, calculated from AME2020 atomic masses. The common roughly 200 MeV figure is a typical total that also includes energy from later product decays; those decays are not shown here.

Gold particles are protons and blue particles are neutrons. Nuclei have no electron shells in this view. Nucleons are mixed schematically throughout each nucleus; their drawn positions are not a model of nuclear structure. Each 30-second demonstration is artificially slowed and repeats with fresh reactants; it is not a chain reaction. Approach, an intermediate excited nucleus, outgoing products, and review are shown separately. Reactants and products use a common center-of-mass frame, with mass-number approximations for recoil. The stage timings are independent teaching intervals, not physical reaction times. The fusion products move oppositely in the center-of-mass frame with a neutron-to-helium speed ratio of about 4:1 (nonrelativistic mass-number approximation), corresponding to about 14.1 and 3.5 MeV. Fission uses one schematic momentum-balanced product configuration, not a predicted energy spectrum or neutron emission geometry. The drawings are not quantum reaction dynamics or a reactor model.

The displayed Q value is Δmc²: fusion Δm ≈ 0.018883 u, fission Δm ≈ 0.186022 u, with 1 u·c² ≈ 931.494 MeV. This is the available energy for the specified ground-state channel, not a predicted fragment energy spectrum. Mass data: IAEA / AME2020. Background: US Department of Energy ↗
